title: What If Killer Bees Escaped a Lab? They Did in 1957, and They're Still Spreading

scenes.text: What if killer bees escaped a lab? In 1957, 26 colonies did. They never stopped.
A Brazilian geneticist was crossing African and European bees to make better honey. A careless beekeeper let 26 colonies out.
The hybrids respond to threats ten times faster, send out ten times more bees, and chase you a quarter mile or more.
They spread up to 200 miles a year. Through Brazil, up Central America, into Mexico.
In 1990, 33 years later, they crossed into Texas. Arizona by 1993, California by 1995. Around 1,000 people died in Brazil alone.
Their venom is no stronger than a normal bee's. There are just far more stings. One mistake with 26 hives changed two continents.

description:
What if killer bees escaped a lab? In 1957, 26 colonies of African honey bees left an experimental apiary about 100 miles from Sao Paulo, Brazil, where they had been imported to breed a better tropical honey bee.
Their hybrid descendants react to disturbance about ten times faster than European honey bees, attack with ten times as many stings and chase intruders for a quarter mile or more. Spreading up to 200 miles a year, they reached Texas in 1990, Arizona in 1993 and California in 1995; the Smithsonian estimates about 1,000 deaths in Brazil.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: The first death in the United States came in 1993, three years after the bees crossed the border. Which accidental release should we run through next? Drop your own what-if below.
